title: A Non-Freaked Out, Focused Approach to the Common Core — Part 3 — Close Reading
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: In the third part of his 'non-freaked out' Common Core series, Stuart (drawing heavily on colleague Erica Beaton's work) tries to rescue close reading from the hype and misinformation surrounding R.CCR.1. He defines it plainly as careful interpretation of a text, attending to how ideas unfold, usually with annotation to slow the reader down. The justification is practical: students are now asked to read appropriately complex texts, so many will struggle, and close reading is the move skilled readers adopt intuitively in college to interpret hard passages, stay on purpose and leave 'bread crumbs' for later writing or discussion. He stresses that not everything should be close read, since doing so would kill a love of reading. Following Schmoker's Focus, he describes a sequence of vocabulary, purpose-setting, modeled thinking, partner practice, checking for understanding and independent practice. His central claim is that close reading in isolation makes no sense: it must always 'bounce pass' into discussion, debate or argumentative writing.
points: Stuart defends close reading as a practical survival skill for complex texts, the same thing he and Beaton did in college under the name 'write in the book so you don't fail.'
He warns that close reading everything, including recreational reading, would kill the 'book love' teachers cultivate elsewhere in the curriculum.

His lesson sequence, adapted from Schmoker's Focus, moves from at most ten pre-taught vocabulary words and a clear purpose through teacher modeling and partner practice to independent close reading at least twice a week.
The post's core claim is that close reading must always feed an authentic intellectual task such as discussion, debate or argumentative writing, never be done just because.
quotes: As with most hyped stuff, there's a lot of misinformation out there about close reading, a lot of “beating texts with a hose” just for the sake of doing it, stuff that confuses kids and makes reading weird and unnatural.

If you came into our classes and asked our students what close reading is, what they'd probably describe is something that can be boiled down to this: the careful interpretation of a text wherein readers pay close attention to the way ideas unfold as they read. Often, this involves annotating texts for the sake of slowing ourselves down and recording our thinking so that we can do cool stuff with what you read.

We ask students to closely read because we ask them to read texts that are appropriately complex for their grade level, and that means that many of our students are going to struggle. When Erica and I started college, we began close reading intuitively, but we called it something like “write in the book so you don't fail.

Kids understand that we don't close read everything; we don't close read recreational reading, for example. Close reading everything would kill a love for reading, and “book love” is something that we try to cultivate in our students through other aspects of our curriculum.

Essentially, close reading is a specific skill that we believe will help our kids practice understanding and using complex texts for diverse purposes. In other words, we provide students with repeated close reading opportunities so that they can flourish in the long-term, no matter what path they take.

Close reading in isolation makes no sense at all. After all, at no point when we naturally learned to close read did we simply do it “because.” We did it to help us pwn intellectual, text-based tasks like discussion and argument, both written and spoken.
